why: The HTTP 409 a refused write is answered with. Read by a Go test and a vitest test, so a field renamed on one side without the other turns the other side red. A drift here is silent in production: the client stops recognising the refusal, falls through to a generic error, and the write is retried forever.
why_two_codes: Both are a 409 carrying a `rejected` array and they are told apart on `error` alone. A lock conflict means the write is blocked and can still succeed later, so its queue is kept; a revision conflict means the document moved and the write can never succeed as sent, so its queue is dropped. Reading one as the other loses work or loops forever.

fields.error: The discriminator. A body whose error is not `revision_conflict` is not one, whatever else it carries.
fields.collection: Which collection the refused documents belong to.
fields.saved: How many of the batch landed. A batch in which one document moved writes the others, so a 409 does not mean nothing happened.
fields.rejected[].docID: The job id the client sent, not the owner-scoped stored id. Named docID to match every other document-scoped payload, including the lock conflict this endpoint also answers.
fields.rejected[].expected: The revision the client's write named in its filter.
fields.rejected[].current: The revision the document carries now, for the client to reconcile against. Zero when the document is gone.
fields.rejected[].gone: The document no longer exists, so there is nothing to reconcile against. Always present, including when false, because a client branches on it and an absent flag would be one more state to decide about.
